newsitem.title: UK: Improved ventilation helps "sick building" - study.
newsitem.headline: Improved ventilation helps "sick building" - study.

text.p: Improving ventilation helps office workers suffering from "sick building syndrome," Canadian researchers reported on Wednesday.

Employees who complained of allergies, eye problems and stress found their problems decreased significantly when they moved to buildings with better air intake, designated smoking areas and separate rooms for copiers, the researchers said.
Dr Jean Bourbeau of McGill University in Montreal surveyed 1,300 workers in 1991, 1992 after they moved offices and again in 1995. They were also examined for symptoms.

Their first buildings had an average fresh air intake of 2.4 litres per second per person as compared to the recommended intake of 10 litres. The new buildings had intakes of 15 to 25 litres, Bourbeau's group reported in the journal Occupational and Environmental Medicine.
The new buildings also had higher humidity, designated smoking areas and separate rooms for photocopiers -- which can produce an irritating dust. Each floor had an independent ventilation system.
A 40 to 50 percent decrease in sick building symptoms was maintained three years later, even if job stress and noise had increased, the doctors reported.
In 1993 McGill researchers found that fresh air alone was not enough to ease the symptoms.

Sick building syndrome was officially recognised by the World Health Organisation in 1982 and defined as an excess of work-related skin and mucous membrane irritations, headache, fatigue and difficulty concentrating. It affects millions of office workers.
